pedagogy.summary: At Key Stage 3 children use faces, edges, vertices and cross-sections to reason about solids and solve problems. The ideas are best taught by physically slicing solids (clay, play-doh, food) at different orientations so the cut face is seen to CHANGE, insisting that a cross-section is a new surface distinct from a pre-existing face, and scaffolding straight (orthogonal) cuts before slanted (oblique) ones. Linking a prism's constant cross-section to its 'base times height' structure connects properties to measurement.
bestPractices: Physically slice solids at parallel, perpendicular and oblique orientations; predict-then-cut so a naive prediction can be violated.
Name the cut as a NEW surface — the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid — distinct from an outer face the solid already had.
Scaffold orthogonal cuts before oblique ones: straight slices can be solved by recognising a shape, slanted slices need more precise reasoning (Cohen & Hegarty; Munns et al.).
Count faces, edges and vertices on the solid handled in the round, not on the 2-D picture, so hidden elements are included.
Treat a prism as a constant cross-section swept along its length, linking to volume as area of base times height.
keyRepresentations: Sliced play-doh or food solids showing the fresh cut face
The cylinder's three cuts: circle (parallel), rectangle (perpendicular), ellipse (oblique)
A prism shown as its cross-section swept through a height
A face/edge/vertex tally taken from the solid in the round
commonMisconceptions: A solid has one fixed cross-section — a cylinder is 'always a circle' whatever the slice.
Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face, reporting a surface the solid already had.
Assumes a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse (over-applying 'the slice looks like the base').
Counts only the faces and edges visible in a 2-D drawing, missing hidden ones.

learn.summary: Learners build the idea that a cross-section is a NEW surface created where a slicing plane meets a solid, so its shape depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid. Core work is predict-then-slice on real solids (play-doh, carrot, food) at parallel, perpendicular and oblique orientations, naming the cut as distinct from any outer face the solid already had, scaffolding straight cuts before slanted ones, transferring the idea to a new solid such as a cone, counting faces/edges/vertices on the solid handled in the round, and linking a prism's constant cross-section to area-of-base-times-height.

activities.title: Predict, then slice: a cylinder gives more than a circle
feedback: If you answered 'circle' for the top-to-bottom cut too, slice the cylinder both ways and lay the two fresh faces side by side: the parallel cut is a circle, the perpendicular (top-to-bottom) cut is a rectangle — the shape tracks the direction of the cut.

If you named the cylinder's flat end or curved outer surface, hold up the freshly cut face and note: 'this surface did not exist before the cut' — the cross-section is new, not a face the solid already had.

The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part: a mismatch between your justification and the real cut is exactly what shows the idea shifting from 'the solid has one cross-section' to 'the shape depends on how you slice it'.
activities.rationale: Predicting then violating a naive prediction targets the dominant misconception that a solid has a single fixed cross-section; students are documented to find identifying cross-section shapes difficult, so making the slice-dependence concrete addresses that difficulty directly.
sourceClaims: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
learnerActions: Hold a play-doh or carrot cylinder and a plastic knife.
BEFORE cutting, predict AND justify the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle; write or say the reason.

Cut and compare the fresh cut face to your prediction (for a true cylinder a rectangle appears, not a circle; a real carrot that tapers gives a near-trapezium, an approximation to the ideal rectangle).
Make a second cut parallel to the circular ends and check that this one does give a circle.
State in your own words why the two cuts give different shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so one solid yields many cross-sections depending on how it is sliced; a cylinder is only 'a circle' when sliced parallel to its base.

activities.title: Tilt the cut: straight before slanted
feedback: If you insisted the tilted cut is still a circle, overlay it on a traced circle: the cut face is longer in one direction. If the cut crossed only the curved surface it is an ellipse, not a circle; if it also clipped a flat end, it is part of an ellipse with a straight edge.

Notice the pattern: straight (orthogonal) cuts can often be solved by recognising a familiar shape, but slanted (oblique) cuts need you to reason about how the plane passes through the solid, so tackle the straight cuts first and build up to slanted ones.
On the cone, a vertical cut through the apex gives a triangle, not a circle — the same lesson that the shape depends on how the plane passes through the solid.
activities.rationale: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones because people assume 2-D shapes extend orthogonally into 3-D; scaffolding from orthogonal to oblique sections, and transferring to a fresh solid, is an evidence-based ordering.
sourceClaims: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones; people tend to assume a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D even for oblique sections, so orthogonal slices can be solved by recognising a shape while oblique slices need metric reasoning — interventions should scaffold from orthogonal to oblique cross-sections.
learnerActions: After solving the parallel and perpendicular cuts, tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant.
Predict first: is the slanted cut face still a circle? Name the shape you expect.
Cut, then lay the slanted cut face over a traced circle of the same cylinder to compare.

Describe how the oblique cut stretches the circle into an ellipse when the slanted plane crosses only the curved surface. If your cut also runs through a flat end, the face is part of an ellipse with a straight edge, so note which case you got.
Transfer the idea to a new solid: predict then check the cross-section of a cone sliced vertically through its apex (a triangle), to test slice-dependence on a different shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Assuming a 2-D shape extends straight up into 3-D leads to calling a slanted cut a circle; oblique cuts need more careful reasoning than straight ones, a slanted slice of a cylinder that crosses only the curved surface is an ellipse (one that also cuts an end is an ellipse cut off by a straight edge), and the slice-dependence idea transfers to other solids such as a cone.

activities.title: The sweep that makes a prism
feedback: If you expected the shape to change along the prism, your repeated cuts parallel to the end show the same triangle each time. A constant polygonal cross-section like this is the defining feature of a prism.
Connect this to measurement: because the cross-section (the base) is the same all the way through, the volume is the area of that base multiplied by the length.
activities.rationale: Linking the constant cross-section of a prism to base-area-times-height connects spatial properties to volume and addresses the documented blending of surface-area and volume ideas.
sourceClaims: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
learnerActions: Take a triangular prism (or model one in play-doh).
Slice it parallel to its triangular end, then slice again further along its length.
Compare the cut faces: check whether the cross-section ever changes along the length.
Explain why a polygonal cross-section that never changes (for slices parallel to the end) is what makes the solid a prism, and connect this to volume as area of the end (base) times the length.
activities.intendedInsight: A prism is a constant polygonal cross-section swept along its length; this constancy (which a cylinder shares, with a circle as its cross-section) links the solid's properties to volume = area of base x height.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices in the round
feedback: If you gave a triangular prism four faces, or missed the back edges, you were counting only what the picture shows — turn the solid over and mark each face as you count to include the hidden ones (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Use the solid itself, not the drawing, as your source of truth for counting.
activities.rationale: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram, which underlies counting only the visible faces and edges of a pictured solid.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram, which underlies counting only the visible faces/edges of a pictured solid.
learnerActions: Hold the actual solid (triangular prism, square-based pyramid) and turn it over in your hands.
Count faces, edges and vertices, marking each face as you tally it so you do not miss hidden ones.
Compare your in-the-round count with what you would have counted from a flat 2-D picture of the same solid.
State how many elements the drawing would have hidden.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting from the solid handled in the round includes hidden faces, edges and vertices that a 2-D drawing conceals, so property-based reasoning must override the 'look' of a diagram.

activities.title: Explore slicing on a rotatable 3-D model (optional scaffold)
feedback: Watch the moment the circle stretches into an ellipse as you tilt the plane away from flat (parallel) towards a slant. The shape is responding continuously to the plane, so 'a cylinder is always a circle' cannot hold.

If a live 3-D model is unavailable, a side-view slider that redraws the cut face as you tilt a cutting plane, or a static reference image of a cylinder's three labelled cuts (circle/rectangle/ellipse) with each cut tappable to reveal its shape, can serve as lighter-weight versions — these summarise the idea but do less to build the felt slice-dependence than hands-on cutting.

Any on-screen or modelled cut face represents an idealised zero-thickness surface; the real play-doh or card slice has slight thickness, so treat it as an approximation to the mathematical cross-section.
activities.rationale: Cross-sections are inherently spatial, and a continuously morphing cut face makes orientation-dependence explicit; a rotatable model complements physical cutting. This is offered as a proposal, not as evidence that any one medium is uniquely necessary.
learnerActions: On a 3-D model, grab a translucent cylinder and a rotatable slicing plane.
Rotate the plane from flat (parallel) to upright (perpendicular) to a slant, watching the cut face render in real time.

Observe how the cut face changes continuously as the plane tilts. Going from flat to upright, the circle stretches into ellipses, then into ellipses cut off by straight edges once the plane meets the ends, and finally becomes a rectangle when the plane is upright.
Keeping the plane parallel to the prism's end, sweep it along the prism's length and watch the cross-section stay constant.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the cut face morph continuously as a plane tilts makes the slice-dependence vivid: one solid, many cross-sections, the shape tracking the tilt of the plane.

constraints: Hands-on cutting is the core method; the 3-D model, 2-D slider and labelled reference image are scaffolds or summaries, useful for illustration but not a replacement for predicting and cutting real solids.

A static or interactive picture can illustrate the three cuts but does not let the learner vary the slice themselves; a quiz that matches cuts to orientations or counts elements of pictured solids checks recognition only and does not itself elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals the misconception.
Scaffold straight (orthogonal) cuts before slanted (oblique) ones; oblique cuts are harder and should not be the entry point.
Always require counting from the solid handled in the round (or a model that can be rotated), not from a single 2-D drawing, so hidden elements are included.

Paper or card cutouts and play-doh slices have real thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness cross-section, and label any on-screen cut face as a model of that idealised surface. Ask about the mathematical surface represented, not whether the physical slice can be held.
Insist the cross-section is named as a NEW surface where the plane meets the solid, distinct from any pre-existing outer face.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices; the legacy error-pattern example of 'four faces' is the mistaken answer, not the correct count — the correct count is stated in activity feedback and the mistaken one is kept only as a diagnostic signal.

Self-audit: a perpendicular (top-to-bottom through the middle) cut of a right cylinder gives a rectangle; a cut parallel to the circular ends gives a circle; a slanted cut across the body gives an ellipse (an oblique cut that reaches a circular end can give part of an ellipse/stadium, but for the straightforward body slant an ellipse is correct for this age group). A vertical cone cut gives a triangle only when it passes through the apex; off-apex it is a hyperbola.

Activity 1's rationale was tightened to cite only the documented difficulty of identifying cross-section shapes; the National Curriculum claim had already been removed from its sourceClaims because it establishes KS3 placement of cross-sections (topic), not the predict-then-slice teaching principle. The volume/surface-area blending content is carried by Activity 3 where the source directly supports it.
Transfer to a cone/new solid was restored (from responseLevels 'full' and the evidence statement) to preserve testing of slice-dependence on a second solid.

The source claims support general teaching principles (difficulty of cross-section identification, orthogonal-before-oblique scaffolding, coordinating spatial and property reasoning); they do not establish that any specific medium (3-D model vs physical cutting) is comparatively more effective, so no such comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.

The legacy row marked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and dialogue as unable to convey spatial slicing; these catalog fit rankings have been removed and the 3-D model reframed as an optional scaffold rather than a necessity.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a play-doh (or carrot) cylinder and a plastic knife. BEFORE any cut, ask them to predict and JUSTIFY the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle. Most predict 'a circle' because a cylinder 'is' a circle. Then cut: a rectangle appears. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part — the mismatch forces the shift from 'the solid has one cross-section' to 'the shape depends on how you slice it'.
probeDeeper: Now I tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant — is the cut face still a circle? What is it?
Is the shape you named a face the cylinder already had, or a new surface the cut made?
A triangular prism is sliced parallel to its triangular end all along its length — does the cut shape ever change? Why does that make it a prism?
How many faces does this prism have altogether, including the ones you cannot see in the picture?
assess.correctAnswer: The parallel cut gives a circle; the top-to-bottom (perpendicular) cut gives a rectangle. A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so it depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid — the cylinder is not 'a circle' by nature, only when sliced parallel to its base.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a solid has a single fixed cross-section — 'a cylinder is a circle', so any cut is a circle regardless of direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slice a play-doh cylinder both ways so the rectangle appears; name the slicing plane and vary its direction explicitly
errorPatterns.distractor: A circle — the same shape as the flat slice
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'circle' for the perpendicular cut too and cannot explain the difference

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face — reports a surface the solid already has rather than the newly cut shape
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut a solid and hold up the fresh face: 'this surface did not exist before the cut'; contrast it with the outer faces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the cylinder's flat end or curved surface instead of the cut face

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes a 2-D shape extends straight (orthogonally) into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse — over-applying 'the slice looks like the base'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slice at a slant and lay the ellipse over a traced circle; scaffold from straight cuts to slanted ones
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the oblique probe insists the tilted cut is still a circle

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the faces, edges and vertices visible in the 2-D drawing, missing the hidden ones
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the solid to turn over and count, marking each face as it is tallied
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a triangular prism four faces, or misses the back edges, when counting from a picture

responseLevels.gap: Gives one shape for every cut ('a circle'), or names an existing face; treats the cross-section as a fixed property of the solid.
responseLevels.full: Explains a cross-section as the intersection of the slicing plane with the solid, so its shape depends on the cut's direction; predicts circle, rectangle and ellipse for the three orientations and links a prism's constant cross-section to its structure, transferring to a cone or a new solid.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the parallel (circle) and perpendicular (rectangle) cuts and can count faces, edges and vertices, but lists these as separate facts — cannot yet say the cut depends on the slicing plane and fails the oblique case (calls it a circle).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A solid cylinder — like a tin of beans — is cut straight across, parallel to its circular ends: what 2-D shape is the freshly cut face? Now the same cylinder is cut straight down through the middle, from top to bottom: what shape is that cut face? Explain why the two cuts give different shapes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands a cross-section as slice-dependent gives two different shapes and can say why; a child holding 'a cylinder's cross-section is a circle' answers 'circle' for both and cannot justify a difference. The reason-tier is essential — answering 'rectangle' by luck without the slicing-plane idea is exposed by the oblique probe, where they revert to 'circle'.

sources.claim: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
sources.source: Dorko & Speer (2013), 'Calculus Students' Understanding of Volume', Investigations in Mathematics Learning 6(2) (ERIC EJ1052960)

sources.claim: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones; people tend to assume a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D even for oblique sections, so orthogonal slices can be solved by recognising a shape while oblique slices need metric reasoning — interventions should scaffold from orthogonal to oblique cross-sections.

sources.claim: Using properties of 3-D shapes including visualising cross-sections is a Key Stage 3 geometry objective in the English National Curriculum.
